chapters.title: Chapter 16: Biology, the Criminal Justice System, and (Oh, Why Not?) Free Will

assets.visual_frame_description: A brain cutaway rendered as a bunker complex: a tiny control-panel operator sits at the console while case files slide past, each annotated with which dials his purview supposedly covers and which biological fuses blow his circuits.
assets.player_mission: Scan a line of legal doctrines and criminal cases and detect the hidden homunculus in each one: the little man in the bunker who, in mitigated free will, overrides seizures but not hypoglycemia. For each stance - M'Naghten rule, causation-versus-compulsion, 'you must be so smart,' the Libet veto - name where the homunculus is presumed to act.
key_concepts: Hardly anyone believes in complete free will - fewer than a thousandth of a percent would convict a person convulsing in a grand mal seizure of assault - and the West has crossed a line embodied in 'It's not him. It's his disease'

From two to seven centuries ago, prosecution of animals, objects, and corpses was commonplace - in a 1457 trial of a pig and her piglets for eating a child, the pig was convicted and executed while the piglets were found too young to be responsible

The M'Naghten rule, formalized after Daniel M'Naghten's 1842 killing of Edward Drummond, finds someone innocent by reason of insanity if he is so 'laboring under such a defect of reason from disease of the mind' that he cannot distinguish right from wrong

John Hinckley Jr. was found not guilty by reason of insanity in his 1981 attempted assassination of Reagan, prompting states to ban the M'Naghten criterion and Congress to pass the 1984 Insanity Defense Reform Act
Mitigated free will is a kind of libertarian dualism - a well-intentioned spirit, a homunculus in a concrete bunker, that can be thwarted by flesh that is sufficiently weak
Even if 99.99 percent of your actions are biologically determined, claiming to have chosen freely even once tacitly invokes a homunculus operating outside the rules of science

Roper v. Simmons (2005) ruled you can't execute someone for a crime committed before age eighteen, and Graham v. Florida (2010) and Miller v. Alabama (2012) banned life without parole for juveniles because their still-developing brains give them the highest potential for reform
Scalia dissented that it is 'absurd to think that one must be mature enough to drive carefully... to be mature enough to understand that murdering another human being is profoundly wrong'

The APA filed briefs emphasizing adolescent brain immaturity in Roper and adolescent maturity to choose abortion without parental consent - Steinberg's resolution: abortion involves slow deliberative reasoning over days, while shooting someone involves impulse control over seconds

The Libet experiment: readiness potentials from the motor cortex appeared about half a second before the reported time of conscious intent to move - and Libet himself proposed the lag offers the potential to consciously veto, 'free won't' (Ramachandran)
Cantor's Sandusky-era argument: 'One cannot choose to not be a pedophile, but one can choose to not be a child molester' - assigning destructive urges to biology and resistance to homuncular grit

The view that assigns aptitude to biology and effort to free will is the most permeating and destructive stance of mitigated free will - 'You must have worked so hard' is as much a property of the physical universe as 'You must be so smart'

assets.visual_frame_description: A courtroom that shifts centuries: the 1563 witch bench dissolves into a modern trial where a brain scan of frontal damage floats before the jury while a prosecutor's questions hammer the expert's inability to predict individual behavior.
assets.player_mission: Play both sides of the witch-reform debate: Johann Weyer arguing in 1563 that elderly women with atrophied tear ducts shouldn't be torched, and the inquisitor insisting the tear test is sound. Then cross-examine a modern courtroom as the defense neuroscientist explaining frontal damage, and take the prosecutor's turn grilling the expert about why brain science can't predict which damaged person becomes a killer.
key_concepts: In 1563 Johann Weyer's De Praestigus Daemonum accepted the existence of witches and the tear test, but warned that elderly women with atrophied lachrymal glands couldn't cry tears - make sure you're not torching a poor elderly person simply because her tear ducts don't work anymore; the book was banned by both the Catholic Church and leading Reformation clergy
Nearly 350 people - 20 of them on death row, imprisoned an average of fourteen years - have been exonerated by DNA fingerprinting according to the Innocence Project
An IQ of 70 or higher is the standard for being smart enough to be executed, a debate pertinent to about 20 percent of people on death row
The belief that schizophrenia is a biological disorder makes jurors less likely to convict schizophrenics but more likely to view them as incurably dangerous

Stephen Morse, the definitive skeptic of neurolaw, has diagnosed 'brain overclaim syndrome' - sufferers infected and inflamed by stunning advances make moral and legal claims the neuroscience cannot sustain
Morse calls neuroscience 'determinism du jour... the only thing different about neuroscience is that we have prettier pictures and it appears more scientific'
Hilary Bok: 'The claim that a person chose her action does not conflict with the claim that some neural processes or states caused it; it simply redescribes it'

Causal data are the gold standard: transcranial magnetic stimulation that transiently activates or inactivates cortex changes moral decision making, decisions about punishment, and levels of generosity and empathy

In the hypothetical cross-examination, the defense neuroscientist must admit that not every person with childhood frontal damage becomes a murderer, or even engages in serious criminal behavior - brain science cannot explain why the same damage produced murder in this defendant

A fractured leg predicts trouble walking at close to 100 percent, and frontal damage predicts something behaviorally odd after a five-minute conversation at about 75 percent - but whether that person will do something horrifically violent is under 50 percent, often way under

Predicting depression: knowing the serotonin transporter gene gives about 10 percent predictive power; adding childhood adversity about 25 percent; adding living alone in poverty maybe 40 percent; adding glucocorticoids, culture, and menstruation pushes maybe above 50 percent - not different amounts of biological causation, different types
Marvin Minsky defined free will as 'internal forces I do not understand' - which must be amended to 'internal forces I do not understand yet'

assets.visual_frame_description: A courtroom gallery rendered as a rewards lab: each verdict emits a readout of which brain circuits fired, while a 'punishment as virtue' gauge shows centuries of epilepsy-style cases where virtuous punishment was successfully abolished.
assets.player_mission: Audit a courthouse's punishment machinery and log every motive for penalizing a defendant: protection, rehabilitation, deterrence, or the frothy limbic pleasure of justice served. For each sentence handed down, trace the neural signature - dIPFC culpability, vmPFC-amygdala-insula punishment froth, dopaminergic reward - and flag which punishments are virtues and which are merely satisfying.
key_concepts: Decision making about culpability for a norm violation correlates with activity in the cognitive dIPFC, while decision making about appropriate punishment activates the emotional vmPFC along with the amygdala and insula - the more activation, the more punishment
When subjects punish someone for a lousy offer in an economic game, there's activation of dopaminergic reward systems - punishment that feels just feels good
The more dopaminergic activation during no-cost punishment in an economic game, the more someone would pay to punish in the other condition

Punishment is effortful and costly - from forgoing a reward in the Ultimatum Game to tax dollars paying for the prison guard who operates the lethal injection machine - and the rush of self-righteous pleasure drives us to shoulder the costs

Morris Hoffman's The Punisher's Brain reviews why we punish: punishment fosters cooperation, it is in the fabric of the evolution of sociality, and it can feel good to be part of a righteous crowd at a public hanging

Rejecting free will doesn't mean doing nothing about criminals - people must be protected from the dangerous, as you wouldn't allow a car with faulty brakes to be driven (Greene and Cohen: for the law, neuroscience changes nothing and everything)
Precluding free will precludes punishment being an end in and of itself - punishment imagined to 'balance' the scales of justice must go, though instrumental punishment and deterrence may remain

We have done it before: once people with epilepsy were virtuously punished for intimacy with Lucifer, now we simply ban them from driving when seizures aren't controlled - and no one views the driving ban as virtuous or pleasurable

In the 1487 Malleus Maleficarum, Kramer and Sprenger identified convulsions - the Gospel of Mark's demon-seized boy - as a sure marker of a witch, and the book's printing-press propagation helped fuel the persecution of an estimated 100,000 to a million people as witches

In the future, people will look back at us as we look back at purveyors of leeches, bloodletting, and trepanation and the fifteenth-century witch experts - 'My God, the things they didn't know then. The harm that they did'

Judges adjudicating trials need the humility of archaeology - as with the terra-cotta army, of which less than 1 percent has been uncovered in more than forty years - and above all else shouldn't act irrevocably

Words like 'evil' and 'soul' should become as irrelevant in courtrooms as in an auto repair shop - an evil car is just one whose internal forces we do not understand yet, and treating damaged humans as broken machines is far more humane than demonizing them as sinners

assets.visual_frame_description: A judge's chambers where each case file lands on a sorting wheel with five bins - full responsibility, caused, compelled, mitigated, excused - while homunculus icons on the wall show which dials each defense knocks loose.
assets.player_mission: Sort a docket of legal defenses - seizures, psychosis, auditory hallucinations, adolescent impulse, childhood frontal damage, addiction, hunger at sentencing - and classify each as excuse, compulsion, mitigation, or no defense at all. Apply the causation-versus-compulsion distinction and the group-level-arbitrary-boundary logic of Roper v. Simmons to each case.
key_concepts: Proponents of mitigated free will distinguish causation from compulsion: every behavior is caused, but only a subset are really, really caused by something that compromises rational deliberative processes

Courts differ on schizophrenic delusions: a voice suggesting a crime is 'caused' but not excusing, while thundering choruses of taunting voices with baying hellhounds are deemed a compulsion - more excusable
David Berkowitz's 'Son of Sam' defense - that his neighbor's dog commanded him to murder - failed, and he was convicted and given six consecutive life sentences

Adolescence arguments cut both ways: group-level attributes with arbitrary age boundaries are accepted for voting, drinking, and driving because you can't test every teenager - but O'Connor wrote that the fact juveniles are generally less culpable doesn't mean a 17-year-old murderer cannot be sufficiently culpable to merit the death penalty

Even Morse concedes: 'Suppose we could show that the higher deliberative centers in the brain seem to be disabled... we've learned something that might be relevant to the legal ascription of responsibility'
The line-drawing problem is practical: a large percentage of death row inmates have a history of damage to the frontal cortex, particularly the most disabling type - early in life

Gazzaniga's 'free will is an illusion, but you're still responsible for your actions' places responsibility 'at a different level of organization: the social level' - which Sapolsky calls either practicality or a social homunculus, since our social world is as much a product of determined brains as simple motor movements
Morse: 'Brains don't kill people. People kill people.' and 'Causation is neither an excuse per se nor the equivalent of compulsion, which is an excusing condition'
The prosecutor's cross-examination reveals neuroscience's core limitation: we still can't predict much about individual behavior - at best at the statistical level of groups
Dweck's praise studies: praising kids for hard work makes them work harder and value the accomplishment for its own sake, while 'you must be so smart' makes effort seem suspect and beneath them

Wilma Rudolph - crippled by polio, worked through the pain, became the fastest woman in the world - feels inspiring in a way natural pole-vaulting talent feels merely impressive, though both rest on the same multifactorial biology

A list of things that influence the homunculus side of the ledger: blood glucose, family-of-birth socioeconomic status, concussive head injury, sleep, prenatal environment, stress hormones, pain, Parkinson's medication, perinatal hypoxia, dopamine D4 receptor variants, frontal stroke, childhood abuse, cognitive load, MAO-A variants, parasites, Huntington's, lead in tap water, individualist or collectivist culture, an attractive woman nearby, and the sweat of a frightened person

assets.visual_frame_description: A sunlit brunch table that fades into a cathedral of causality: the praised pineapple floats above a web of genes, cultural values, and socioeconomic luck, while a two-sided scoreboard tracks whether you credit free will for virtues but biology only for vices.
assets.player_mission: Confront the final, hardest test of denying free will: accepting that your best traits - talents, willpower, creativity, decency - are as biologically determined as your worst. Stand at the brunch table where your host is being praised for choosing a perfect pineapple, and decide whether to explain zygomatic arches and olfactory receptors - or save the heavy lifting of rational thought for when you judge others harshly.
key_concepts: If we deny free will for the worst of our behaviors, the same must apply to the best - talents, willpower, creativity, decency, and compassion
It should seem as ludicrous to take credit for your talents as to thank someone for praising your free will instead of explaining how mechanical forces acted on your zygomatic arches

In the pineapple anecdote, the host's supposed free will is actually genes for olfactory receptors, deep cultural values about choosing fruit, and the sheer luck of a socioeconomic trajectory that allows prowling an overpriced organic market

Daniel Dennett has written about free will 'worth wanting' - if there really is free will, it is getting consigned to domains too mundane to be worth the effort: do I want briefs or boxer shorts today?
If science will accrue any more knowledge, you've committed to free will being eliminated or the homunculus jammed into ever tinier places

Less than two centuries since science learned the frontal cortex has something to do with appropriate behavior; less than seventy years since schizophrenia was found to be a biochemical disorder; about fifty since dyslexia was tied to microscopic cortical malformations; twenty-five since epigenetics was found to alter behavior
Minsky's definition of free will - 'internal forces I do not understand' - explains why people believe in it: most people know next to nothing about those internal forces

Sapolsky concedes he can't imagine living life as if there is no free will, and settles for making sure our homuncular myths are benign and saving truly rational thinking for when we judge others harshly

The 'internal forces' literature is exploding: searches for oxytocin and trust show 193 papers, nearly all recent, and genes-and-behavior searches grew from a handful per decade before 1950 to over 52,000 in 2010-2020
No rational person who rejects free will argues we should do nothing about dangerous people - rehabilitation if possible, containment if not

Sapolsky's proposal 'Should the Criminal Justice System Be Abolished?' grew out of the view that the current system - built on retributive punishment - needs to be replaced with something with utterly different underpinnings
Humans are more humane as broken machines than as sinners - 'internal forces we do not understand yet' beats demonization

assets.visual_frame_description: A telescope aimed back through history: each atrocity shimmers as a data point on a declining violence curve while countervailing wars flare red on the horizon, and a counter re-expresses death tolls per capita and per year of duration.
assets.player_mission: Scan the last five centuries of violence and tag which trends are retreating and which are ascendant: slavery, child labor, homicide rates, capital punishment, weapons bans, proxy wars, lone-wolf terror, and the reach of the violent few. For each sighting, decide whether it supports or challenges Pinker's claim that we live in the most peaceful era of our species.
key_concepts: At the dawn of the nineteenth century slavery occurred worldwide, child labor was universal, and no country punished mistreatment of animals - now every nation has outlawed slavery, most have child labor laws, and most regulate treatment of animals
Fifteenth-century Europe averaged 41 homicides per 100,000 people per year; the world now averages 6.9, Europe 1.4, and Iceland, Japan, and Singapore 0.3

Rarer in recent centuries: forced marriages, child brides, genital mutilation, wife beating, polygamy, widow burning, persecution of homosexuals, epileptics, and albinos, beating of schoolchildren, capital punishment

Invented in the last century: bans on certain types of weapons, the World Court, the concept of crimes against humanity, the UN and multinational peacekeeping, international agreements against trafficking in blood diamonds and ivory, and agencies aiding disaster victims worldwide
Mauritania became the last country to ban slavery in 1981, yet roughly 20 percent of its people are still slaves and the government has prosecuted a total of one slave owner

Pinker's The Better Angels of Our Nature documents that roughly half a million people died in the Roman Colosseum for the pleasure of crowds, and quotes L. P. Hartley: 'The past is a foreign country: they do things differently there'

Pinker's 'Long Peace' - Europe at peace since 1945 except for the Balkan wars - is criticized as Eurocentrism: the West fought on in Indochina, Algeria, Malaya, Kenya, Angola, Mozambique, Afghanistan, Vietnam, Korea, and Latin America, and invented proxy wars
World War II killed 55 million people, and with World War I, Stalin, Mao, and the Russian and Chinese civil wars the twentieth century totals 130 million

When deaths are expressed as a percentage of total population, World War II is the only twentieth-century event in the top ten, behind An Lushan, the Mongol conquests, the Mideast slave trade, the fall of Ming, the fall of Rome, Tamerlane, Native American annihilation, and the Atlantic slave trade

When also corrected for duration, the top ten includes World War II (number one), World War I (number three), the Russian Civil War, Mao, and the Rwandan genocide (number seven) - 700,000 people killed in a hundred days

assets.visual_frame_description: A moonlit no-man's-land strung with barbed wire: soldiers from both trenches converge mid-field with food, tobacco, and an improvised ball, while the far command posts glow with court-martial threats like distant signal lamps.
assets.player_mission: Play both sides of the 1914 Christmas Truce: the British and German soldiers who meet in no-man's-land, and the officers who order them back to killing. Negotiate the shovels, the carols, the soccer match and the shadow of the future - then switch sides and try to sustain a wordless Live and Let Live arrangement under the threat of court-martial.
key_concepts: The Christmas Truce of 1914 began as an agreement to halt hostilities for Christmas dinner and retrieval of the dead, then spread to joint burial services, exchanges of food, drink, and tobacco, group portraits, souvenir exchanges, and soccer matches with improvised balls
One historian records the chilling detail that a German soldier condemned the truce-makers as traitors - an obscure corporal named Hitler

It took officers' threats of court-martial to get soldiers back to fighting, and with only sporadic exceptions the truce never happened again - even brief Christmas truces to retrieve the dead led to court-martials
The truce worked because static trench warfare meant soldiers faced each other day after day, producing a shadow of the future: betray the truce and expect no-holds-barred revenge

The truce was aided by shared Judeo-Christian tradition and Western European culture - calling the enemy 'Fritz' differs completely from the pseudospeciation of Vietnam's 'gooks,' 'slants,' and 'dinks'

Most German soldiers were Saxons expressing cousinly affinity for British Anglo-Saxons (both should fight the Prussians), while Brits perceived themselves as fighting to save the French, their historical enemy
The truce was also aided by top-down approval: officers negotiated, and figures such as the pope called for a truce

In the 'Live and Let Live' phenomenon documented by Tony Ashworth, soldiers repeatedly evolved stable truces without exchanging a word - guns fell silent at shared dinner times and during awful weather, and wagon trains and latrines were spared to prevent reciprocal shelling

Truces were established by ritualization: your best sniper repeatedly put bullets into the same spot on an abandoned house, signaling 'he could have aimed at you instead' - and the other side reciprocated

Live and Let Live survived violations - a gung-ho rookie's shell typically drew exactly two shells back, aimed at important targets, and then peace resumed; Germans once shouted, 'We are very sorry about that... it is that damned Prussian artillery'

Ashworth observed minimal hostility toward the enemy in trench soldiers' diaries - the further from the front, the more hostility: 'Out here, one can respect a brave, skillful, and resourceful enemy. They have people they love at home'
Repeatedly the brass intervened - rotating troops, threatening court-martials, ordering savage raids requiring hand-to-hand combat that shattered any sense of shared interests

assets.topic: Audit: The Contact and Cooperation Field Log
assets.visual_frame_description: A summer-camp field site split into two zones: the contact program's activities glow where equal numbers, neutral settings, and successful shared goals occur, while a follow-up chart shows 91 percent of former campers never staying in touch.
assets.player_mission: Audit an intergroup-contact program - a Seeds of Peace camp, a desegregated workplace, a four-way stop sign - and log every mechanism of cooperation you witness: open-ended play, spillover between games, open-book reputation, costly punishment, and choosing your partner. Score each contact on equal status, shared goals, and institutional oversight, and predict whether the effects will persist after the campers go home.
key_concepts: A 2006 meta-analysis of about five hundred studies comprising over 250,000 subjects from thirty-eight countries concluded that sustained intergroup contact generally decreases prejudice, with beneficial effects roughly equal for race, religion, ethnicity, and sexual orientation

Contact theory works best when groups meet in equal numbers and treatment, in a neutral setting free of agitprop, with institutional oversight - and most of all when there is a shared goal, especially a successful one, which reprioritizes Us/Them dichotomies

Intergroup contact readily elevates hostilities when groups are treated unequally, when the smaller group is surrounded, when boundaries are ambiguous, and when groups vie to display sacred symbols - as with Orangemen marching through Catholic neighborhoods
The workplace is a particularly effective venue: decreased prejudice about Thems at work often generalizes to Thems at large and even to other types of Thems
Contact between a dominant group and a subordinate minority usually decreases prejudice more in the former - the latter have higher thresholds

Seeds of Peace and similar programs produce less fear and more positive views of Thems in the immediate aftermath, but effects are usually transient - in one survey, 91 percent of Palestinian and Israeli teenagers never stayed in touch

Persistent reductions in prejudice usually involve exceptionalism - 'Yes, most Thems are awful, but I hung out with a Them once who was okay' - and no prominent peace activist has emerged from thousands of Seeds of Peace participants
Susan Fiske showed automatic other-race-face amygdala responses can be undone when subjects think of that face as belonging to a person, not a Them

Pumla Gobodo-Madikizela interviewed apartheid death-squad commander Eugene de Kock for over forty hours and reflexively touched his finger between the jail bars - a taboo act showing the tenuous elements of Us-ness dominated at that moment

Fraternizing between enemy soldiers is remarkably frequent in war - most common when they share race and major religion, when they are enlisted men, when individuals rather than groups encounter each other, and when the same person faces you day after day

In the Peninsular War a British sentry was found guarding both armies' muskets because his French counterpart had snuck off to buy liquor for them to share - and in the American Civil War Yankees and Rebels held joint baptismal services the evening before battles

Cooperation mechanisms include open-ended play (an unknown number of rounds creating the shadow of the future), multiple games (psychological spillover from a low-threshold game), open-book play (reputation), and indirect reciprocity, where reputation is the common currency like money

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: The Truth and Reconciliation Classifier
assets.visual_frame_description: A records room where each mechanism is a card slotted into labeled drawers: TRC outcomes tabulate amnesty granted to 13 percent of 6,000-plus applicants, while apology cards light up differently for system-oriented, relational, and autonomous victims.
assets.player_mission: Sort a shelf of post-conflict mechanisms - TRCs, apologies, reparations, amnesty, forgiveness, forgetting - and classify each instance as reconciliation, remorse, forgiveness, or mere pragmatism. Match each apology to its recipient type, and determine which elements the South African TRC actually delivered versus which the tearful-forgiveness myth promised.
key_concepts: The popular perception of truth and reconciliation commissions - perpetrators confess, beg forgiveness, and receive tearful embraces - is wrong: TRCs are typically exercises in pragmatism, where perpetrators vow never to harm again and victims vow not to seek extrajudicial retribution

South Africa's TRC, overseen by Desmond Tutu, had more than six thousand perpetrators testify and apply for amnesty, which was granted to 13 percent - remorse was not required and few showed it, since the goal was to increase the odds the shattered nation would function

Victim participants commonly felt the TRC had been more successful at the national than the local level, and many were outraged at the absence of apologies, reparations, and the persistence of perpetrators in their jobs - including symbols like holidays and street names celebrating apartheid
A wide majority of black (but not white) South Africans saw the TRC as fair and successful, and it accompanied the country's miraculous transition rather than descent into civil war

System-oriented victims respond most to apologies emphasizing failure of the system, relationship-oriented victims to empathic apologies, and autonomous victims to apologies accompanied by offers of compensation

key_concepts: On March 16, 1968, a company under Lieutenant William Calley Jr. killed between 350 and 500 unarmed civilians at My Lai - infants and elderly included - after suffering twenty-eight deaths and injuries from booby traps and meeting no enemy fire
Of the twenty-six soldiers criminally charged over My Lai, only Calley was convicted, sentenced to three years of house arrest - 'just following orders' was the order of the day

Hugh Thompson Jr., descended from Native American survivors of the Trail of Tears and raised to oppose segregation, landed his helicopter between the villagers and the soldiers and ordered his crew to mow the Americans down if they attempted further harm

Thompson's crew members Glenn Andreotta and Lawrence Colburn - observant Catholics - helped evacuate survivors; Andreotta waded through the dead in a ditch to rescue a miraculously unharmed four-year-old

Thompson and Colburn played key roles in making the massacre public, received death threats for years, and were only honored by the military thirty years later; Thompson died in 2006 with Colburn at his bedside

Individual thresholds varied at My Lai: one soldier killed a mother and child then refused to do more; another herded civilians but refused to fire; PFC Michael Bernhardt refused and was placed on more dangerous patrols, perhaps in hopes he'd be killed
